frame: Ruby wrote this story about herself. The Pointern isn't sure it believes her.
text: My name is Ruby Tan, and I am not scared of anything. I would like that written down. When Dad said the old boat shed at the end of the jetty was haunted, I laughed so loudly that a seagull fell off the railing. That night, I decided to prove him wrong. I took a torch. I also took two spare torches, because torches can break, and a cricket bat, because I like cricket. I walked to the shed very slowly, to be polite to the spiders. The door was open. Inside, it smelled like old rope and wet fish. Something dripped in the corner. I stepped inside and shone my torch around, and everything was perfectly normal. Then the wind slammed the door shut behind me. I left through the window, very calmly, at a normal speed for a person who is not scared. I was home in forty seconds. Dad asked why I was out of breath and why I had seaweed in my hair. I said I had been jogging. At midnight. As people do.

frame: The Echobat loves this story so much it recorded the whole thing. The Pointern has a question.

frame: A girl who moved to Twotide Atoll wrote this for the school magazine. The Pointern circled one bit.
text: I have always hated the sea. I want to be clear about that from the start. It is cold, it is wet, it is full of things that sting, and it tastes like a sock that has been pickled. When Mum announced that we were moving to Twotide Atoll, where the sea is everywhere you look, I locked myself in the bathroom for an entire afternoon. Our new house was so close to the water that I could hear it at night, shushing and grumbling, as if it were complaining about me. For the first month, I didn't go near it. Then, one evening, my little brother's kite blew out over the lagoon, and before I could think, I had waded in up to my knees to grab the string. The water was warm. That surprised me so much that I just stood there, holding the kite, while tiny silver fish nibbled at my ankles as if they were checking whether I was edible. A turtle surfaced a few metres away, looked at me with its old, wrinkled face and sank again without a sound. I stayed until the sun went down. I still think the sea tastes like a pickled sock. But now, every evening, I am the first one in the water, and Mum has to drag me out when it gets dark.
prompt: Wren thinks the narrator changes her mind about the sea. Which evidence backs this up?
answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: She starts out hating the sea, but ends up first in the water every evening.
Her little brother's kite blows out over the lagoon.
She learns to surf so she can enter the island's surf contest at the end of summer.
She says the sea tastes 'like a sock that has been pickled'.

text: For two years, Sami and Leo built a video game called Tide Runners in Leo's garage, on a computer they had rescued from the tip. The game had one special level, the Twin Tides, which could only be played with two people at once. They planned to enter it in the Island Game Jam in December. On stage, Sami held up the trophy and pointed at the big screen behind him, where Leo was cheering on a video call from the mainland, at six in the morning, still in his pyjamas. The crowd went wild. frame: Tully wrote a review of a story from the Twotide library. Then the Pointern sat on it.
text: Mei had entered the Twotide Dumpling Contest three times and come last three times. The first year, her dumplings fell apart in the pot. The second year, they were so hard that a judge chipped a tooth. The third year, she forgot the filling altogether. This year, her grandpa, Lu, who hadn't cooked since his hands got shaky, sat beside her at the kitchen bench every night for a month. He couldn't fold the dumplings himself any more, but he watched every fold and told her what she was doing wrong. 'Too much filling. Not enough water on the edge. Pinch, don't squash.' On the night before the contest, Mei burned the whole batch and burst into tears. Grandpa Lu didn't say a word. He just got out the flour and started the dough again, his shaky hands slowly kneading, while Mei wiped her face and started chopping. They worked until midnight. By the end, Grandpa Lu's hands ached so badly that he had to rest them in a bowl of warm water, but he didn't complain once. The next day, Mei's dumplings won first prize. When the judge handed her the trophy, Mei ran straight off the stage and put it in Grandpa Lu's lap.
prompt: Put Tully's review in order: opinion, evidence, why it backs her up, what others might say, then her reply.
answerWith: every item, in the correct order
items: This shows that he keeps going when it's hard for him, so that Mei can win.
However, even Mei seems to agree with me, because she puts the trophy straight into Grandpa Lu's lap.
Some readers might say Mei is the hero, because she is the one who wins first prize.
In my opinion, Grandpa Lu is the real hero of 'The Dumpling Contest'.
The clearest evidence is the night Mei burns the batch, when he starts the dough again with his shaky hands.
